rounds.text: Triumph International Finance India Ltd is heavily discounted by the market, trading at an exceptionally low P/E of 2.89x [E1] compared to a sector benchmark of 19.61x [E5], alongside a P/B of 0x versus a sector benchmark of 1.31x [E6]. This steep mispricing offers a massive margin of safety of 81.8%, as a discounted cash flow model puts intrinsic value at Rs 87 per share against a market price of Rs 15.8 [E28, E29]. Furthermore, underlying fundamentals show tangible momentum, highlighted by a 3-year compounded profit growth of 18% [E14], accelerating earnings growth [E40], and a return on assets of 2.41% that outpaces the sector benchmark of 1.89% [E7]. A reverse DCF indicates that the current share price absurdly implies negative 21.8% earnings growth, ignoring the positive reality of results improving with net profit up 20% year-over-year [E30, E41]. A superficial low P/E ratio of 2.89x [E1] masks severe underlying operational deterioration, most notably demonstrated by a catastrophic -100% compounded sales growth over the trailing twelve months [E12]. This top-line collapse is compounded by negative cash generation, with operating cash flow plunging to Rs -3.91 Cr and free cash flow matching that negative output in Mar 2026 [E20, E21], leading to a dismal -1.00x cash conversion rate [E19]. Furthermore, reported earnings quality is highly suspect because net profit relies on Rs 4.40 Cr of other income [E35], while the core capital-allocation efficiency remains poor with a negative ROE of -5.85% [E8] and a modest ROCE of just 2.3% [E9] or 8.6% [E11]. Balance sheet and ownership risks further cap the investment appeal, highlighted by massive flat borrowings of Rs 114.29 Cr [E23] and a low promoter holding of only 31.5% [E34] sitting near the bottom 11% of its 52-week range [E4]. Conceded: a discounted cash flow model suggests a theoretical intrinsic value of Rs 87 per share [E28], and short-term liquidity appears comfortable with a current ratio of 13.97x [E22].

Conceded: operating and free cash flows stand at Rs -3.91 Cr for Mar 2026 [E20, E21], but short-term liquidity is heavily cushioned by a robust current ratio of 13.97x [E22]. While the bear points to low core efficiency metrics like a negative ROE [E8], the company actually delivers a competitive ROA of 2.41% beating the sector benchmark of 1.89% [E7]. The market heavily overpunishes the stock down at 11% of its 52-week range [E4] despite a deeply discounted reverse DCF implying that the current price anchors on an unrealistic -21.8% earnings decline [E30]. Finally, stale sentiment ignores a fundamental turnaround where recent results score 81/100 and outperform expectations relative to price performance [E32, E41].

Conceded: the 3-year compounded profit growth is 18% and TTM profit growth is 7% [E14, E15]. However, the bull's dismissal of top-line collapse ignores that compounded sales growth over the trailing twelve months has completely cratered to -100% [E12]. While the bull leans on a 13.97x current ratio to excuse cash burn [E22], this liquidity cushion sits alongside a severe operating and free cash flow drain of Rs -3.91 Cr each for March 2026, dragging cash conversion down to an alarming -1.00x [E19, E20, E21]. The bull’s citation of a 2.41% ROA [E7] whitewashes the reality of a deeply negative ROE of -5.85% which trails the sector benchmark of 4.9% [E8], alongside a lackluster ROCE of 2.3% [E9]. Furthermore, the claim that the market is overpunishing the stock near its 52-week low [E4] glosses over the fact that reported earnings are artificially propped up by Rs.4.40 Cr of other income [E35], while total borrowings remain locked at a heavy Rs 114.29 Cr [E23]. Finally, the bull's reliance on turnaround sentiment ignores that the stock's 1-year compounded share price growth is down -41% [E16] and promoter holding is low at just 31.5% [E34].
